slides.title: What the benchmarks measure
slides.caption: A memory benchmark asks questions about a long conversation. There are two ways to score it, and most claims quote one while the reader assumes the other.

slides.title: What we will cover
slides.caption: The two schools of scoring and the six benchmarks that matter. Why two are saturated and the vendor dispute of 2025. Ten ways a score misleads and five questions to ask.

slides.title: The retrieval school: was it found
slides.caption: Retrieval recall at k asks what fraction of the gold evidence sits in the top k results. No answer is generated. The standard form is the TREC fraction.

slides.title: The answer school: was it right
slides.caption: A reader answers from what was retrieved. The answer is scored by word overlap or by a model as judge. It depends on the reader and the judge.

slides.title: Two schools, two tables
slides.caption: Both schools are legitimate. The only error is to place a retrieval-only number beside an answer number and read them as one thing.

slides.title: The six benchmarks that matter
slides.caption: LoCoMo and LongMemEval are saturated. BEAM and MemoryAgentBench are far from it. ConvoMem finds retrieval unnecessary below 150 conversations. LongMemEval-V2 passes ten million tokens.

slides.title: Five more in 2026 say the same
slides.caption: Five benchmarks from February to August 2026 report the same two things. Plain retrieval or plain long context stays competitive. Factual scores do not carry over to using the memory.

slides.title: Why the first benchmark is saturated
slides.caption: A conversation fits inside a modern context window several times over. The scorer's category labels differ from the paper. 446 questions have no answer. 99 labels are wrong.

slides.title: The second benchmark is better built
slides.caption: A fixed judge with 97 percent agreement with humans, seven question types, and separate columns for retrieval and answers. Its authors measured a frontier model at 0.606.

slides.title: The dispute of 2025
slides.caption: The two largest vendors published each other's scores. One reported 65.99. The other corrected its own 84 to 75.14. The first recomputed that to 58.44. The benchmark cannot separate them.

slides.title: Ten ways a score misleads, one to five
slides.caption: Any-hit reported as recall. A k larger than the pool. Retrieval beside judged answers. The credited target. Category relabelling and denominators.

slides.title: Ten ways a score misleads, six to ten
slides.caption: Fixes tuned to named questions. The vendor as reader and judge. Corrupted or missing gold. Single runs. Synthetic recall as a proxy for reading.

slides.title: Five questions before believing a number
slides.caption: Which school? What unit and pool? What k? Whose reader and judge? How many tokens, and does that fit one context window?

slides.title: What to remember
slides.caption: Two schools, two tables. The two famous benchmarks fit in one context window and are saturated. Ten ways a score misleads. Five questions to ask.
